analysis.one_liner: Cuts Medicare payments to hospitals and nursing homes owned by private equity firms or real estate investment trusts.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on March 12, 2026 with three Democratic sponsors and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend Medicare law to bar federal Medicare payments to any hospital or skilled nursing facility owned or controlled by a private equity fund, a company controlled by such a fund, or a real estate investment trust. Facilities already owned by these firms when the law passes would get a three-year grace period to sell or restructure before losing Medicare payments. The goal is to push financial-investment ownership out of hospitals and nursing homes that care for Medicare patients.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who get care at hospitals and nursing homes, and communities where private equity ownership has been linked to staff cuts, higher prices, and facility closures. Independent and nonprofit hospitals also gain competitively if investor-owned competitors exit the market.

how_it_helps.text: No Medicare payment may be made to a hospital or skilled nursing facility owned or controlled by a private equity fund, a firm controlled by such a fund, or a real estate investment trust [S2].
Facilities already owned by covered firms on the date of enactment get a three-year window before the prohibition applies, giving them time to change ownership rather than close abruptly [S2].
Covered firms and their affiliates are jointly and severally liable for any penalty their facilities receive, so the parent investor cannot shield itself behind the local facility [S2].
The definition of control reaches indirect and layered ownership, including any 10 percent or larger voting stake, so a fund cannot evade the rule through intermediaries [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds and real estate investment trusts that own hospitals and nursing homes, and their investors, who would have to sell or restructure those facilities within three years or lose Medicare revenue. Hospitals themselves could face disruption during that transition.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity funds and hospital REITs

drawbacks.text: The three-year cutoff could force a sale or closure at facilities that cannot find a new buyer, and if the investor-owned hospital is the only provider in a community, patients could temporarily lose nearby care [S2].

The ban covers real estate investment trusts, which hold the buildings for many hospitals under sale-leaseback arrangements, so some facilities with otherwise conventional ownership could be swept in and have to unwind long-standing property deals [S2].

Ownership alone is a blunt proxy: it bars Medicare payments from every investor-owned facility, including ones with strong records, rather than targeting facilities where ownership is linked to worse care [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If the concern that investor ownership degrades hospital and nursing home care is right, removing Medicare dollars from those owners is a strong lever, and the three-year grace period and notice-and-hearing protections soften the transition [S2]. The cost is concentrated on the funds and trusts that would have to exit, plus some risk of local disruption during ownership changes. The broad definition that captures REIT-owned property is the biggest design flaw an honest supporter would acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It has been sitting in the Senate Finance Committee since the day it was introduced, with no hearing, markup, or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Murphy introduced the bill on March 12, 2026, joined by Senators Blumenthal and Merkley [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance, which has jurisdiction over Medicare [S4].
No further action has been recorded since the referral [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far the status quo holds: private equity funds and real estate trusts that own hospitals and nursing homes keep collecting Medicare payments with no new restrictions, because the bill has not moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity hospital owners, for now

for.name: Sen. Chris Murphy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar Medicare payments to hospitals and nursing facilities owned by private equity funds or REITs.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has not scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors are Democrats and both cosponsors are Senate Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee led by a Republican chair with no action taken [S3][S4].

industries.industry: Private equity firms that own hospitals and nursing homes
industries.note: They would lose Medicare revenue, the main payer for their hospital and nursing home patients, unless they sold within three years. Their financial model typically relies on debt-funded acquisitions and asset sales at these facilities.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts
industries.note: REITs that own hospital and nursing home property would make their tenants ineligible for Medicare unless the properties changed hands, unwinding the sale-leaseback structures many hospitals depend on.
They would lose investor-owned competitors and could pick up patients and staff if those facilities sell or close.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to Senate Finance with no cosponsors from the majority party and no committee action typically die quietly at the end of a Congress. Unless a Republican cosponsor or a committee hearing materializes, this bill is very unlikely to reach the Senate floor before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027.
